title: The Weak and the Strong: Welcoming Without Judging
summary: Paul addresses believers who disagree about food and special days. Those whose faith allows them to eat anything must not look down on those who abstain, and those who abstain must not condemn those who eat, because God has welcomed both and each will answer to the Lord. Paul himself holds that no food is unclean in itself, but he urges the strong to give up their freedom rather than cause a brother or sister to stumble, since the kingdom of God is about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
story: Chapters 12 and 13 described the life of love that follows from God's mercy. Chapter 14 applies that love to a specific and divisive issue in the Roman church. After eleven chapters in which Paul has argued that Jews and Gentiles are saved on the same basis, by faith, he now shows what that equality looks like when believers from different backgrounds eat together and worship together. The discussion continues through 15:13, where it ends with a vision of Jews and Gentiles glorifying God with one voice. The practical instructions here are the outworking of the letter's theology.
historical:
The disagreements behind this chapter most likely arose from the mixed makeup of the Roman church. Many Jewish believers continued to keep the food laws of the law of Moses and to observe the Sabbath and Jewish festivals, and some Gentile believers who had been attracted to Judaism before becoming Christians may have done the same. Other believers, including many Gentiles and some Jews like Paul, held that these practices were no longer required in Christ. The expulsion of Jews under Claudius around AD 49 and their return after AD 54 may have sharpened these tensions, as Gentile-led households met returning Jewish believers with different habits.

The reference to eating only vegetables (verse 2) has several possible explanations. Jews living in a pagan city could not always be sure that meat sold in the market was prepared according to the law or had not been offered to idols, so some avoided meat altogether, as Daniel and his friends did in Babylon (Daniel 1:8-16). Some interpreters think the issue is mainly Jewish food law; others think it includes wider scruples, such as the concern about idol meat addressed in 1 Corinthians 8 to 10.
cultural:
In the ancient Mediterranean, food was never only food. What a person ate, and with whom, marked identity and belonging. Jewish food laws distinguished Jews from their neighbors, and pagan writers often remarked on Jewish refusal of pork and Sabbath rest. Meat sold in city markets often came from animals sacrificed in temples, and common meals frequently included religious rites. Sharing a meal meant accepting someone as a member of one's group, which is why disputes over food could divide a church.

The word for "unclean" in verse 14 (koinos, literally common) was the ordinary Jewish term for food that was ritually impure. Paul's statement that nothing is unclean in itself echoes Jesus' teaching in Mark 7:15-19, where Mark comments that Jesus declared all foods clean. The observance of days would most naturally refer to the Sabbath and the Jewish festivals, though some think fast days or other calendars may be included.
literary: The chapter is a pastoral argument built around a few repeated verbs: accept, judge, belittle, stand, and stumble. Paul addresses both groups in turn, often in balanced sentences (the one who eats and the one who does not; the one who observes the day and the one who does not). Verses 7 to 12 widen the frame to the lordship of Christ and the final judgment, quoting Isaiah 45:23. Paul then states his own conviction (verse 14) before turning to the strong with a series of warnings about causing others to stumble. The chapter ends with a principle about conscience (verse 23). Some ancient manuscripts place the doxology found at 16:25-27 at the end of this chapter, a sign of the complex early history of the letter's copies.

outline.t: Days and food: living to the Lord
Each will give an account to God
No stumbling block: the kingdom is not food and drink

doctrines.note: The church is a community of people God has welcomed, and its members must welcome each other on the same terms. Disagreements on matters that are not essential should not divide those whom Christ has received.
Each believer will stand before God's judgment seat and give an account to him. That future judgment is a reason to stop judging one another now, since believers are servants of the same master.
The kingdom of God is defined in verse 17 as righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, not eating and drinking. Its values set the priorities for how believers handle their freedom.

words.note: Proslambano, to receive or welcome, often into one's home or company. The chapter opens with the command to accept the one who is weak in faith, and 15:7 closes the discussion by grounding it in Christ's acceptance of believers. The word implies full welcome, not grudging toleration.

Krino, to judge. It appears eight times in this chapter and moves between senses: to pass judgment on others (verses 3, 4, 10, 13), to decide (verse 13), and to regard one day above another (verse 5). Paul plays on the word in verse 13: stop judging one another, but decide instead not to put an obstacle in anyone's way.

Koinos, common, used by Jews to mean ritually unclean. Paul is convinced that nothing is koinos in itself, but that something becomes so for the person who regards it that way. That combination of objective freedom and respect for another's conscience is the heart of his counsel.

christ: Christ's lordship is the ground of the whole chapter. Verses 7 to 9 say that believers live and die to the Lord, and that Christ died and returned to life to be Lord of both the dead and the living. Whatever a believer eats or does not eat, the question is whether it is done to him. The phrase “for whom Christ died” in verse 15 gives every weaker brother or sister immense worth: the strong must not destroy by their eating a person for whom the Lord gave his life. Paul's conviction that nothing is unclean comes "in the Lord Jesus", echoing Jesus' own teaching about food. The quotation of Isaiah 45:23, where every knee bows to God, is applied to the judgment seat of God here, and in Philippians 2:10-11 Paul applies the same verse to Jesus, a sign of how closely he identifies Christ with Israel's God.

hard.q: How do we tell which issues are matters of conscience and which are essential?
hard.a:
Romans 14 is often used to settle disagreements by labeling them matters of preference, but the chapter itself sets limits on that move. The issues Paul treats here, food and days, are matters in which both practices can be done to the Lord with thanksgiving. Elsewhere Paul is not neutral on every question: in Galatians he opposes those who required Gentiles to keep the law in order to be justified, and in Romans 16:17 he warns against those who cause divisions contrary to the teaching. Christians have long distinguished between matters that belong to the heart of the faith and matters on which faithful believers can differ, sometimes called adiaphora, things indifferent.

The difficulty lies in deciding which is which. Some traditions draw the line at the historic creeds; others include more specific teaching on worship, sacraments, or ethics. Romans 14 does not settle every such question, but it gives a test that applies within whatever lines one draws: can both practices be done to the Lord with thanksgiving? If so, believers should not despise or condemn one another over them, and the strong should be ready to limit their freedom for the sake of the weak.

questions: Paul warns the strong not to belittle and the weak not to judge. Which of those temptations comes more naturally to you?
Verse 17 describes the kingdom as righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. What disputes in churches today might look smaller in light of that definition?
When have you given up a freedom for someone else's sake, and when have you insisted on it? What guided your choice?
